result.summary: This chapter traces the royal house of Troy from Dardanus through Ilus, Laomedon and Priam, including the founding of Ilium, the Palladium, and the birth and fate of Paris. It then turns to the river Asopus and his daughter Aegina, whose son Aeacus fathers Peleus and Telamon, and ends with Telamon's line at Salamis.

scenes.title: Dardanus and the Trojan line
scenes.summary: Dardanus leaves Samothrace after Iasion's death, settles in Teucer's land and founds Dardania. His descendants include Tros, Ganymede, who is carried off by Zeus, and Anchises, father of Aeneas.
scenes.stakes: Dardanus must find a new home after his brother's death.

scenes.title: Ilus founds Ilium; the Palladium
scenes.summary: Ilus wins games in Phrygia, follows a cow and founds Ilium, where the Palladium falls from heaven. Its origin is told, then Laomedon's family and Tithonus's love for the Dawn.

scenes.title: Priam, Paris and Oenone
scenes.summary: Priam's wife Hecuba dreams of a firebrand, and the infant Paris is exposed but survives. He grows up, takes Helen, is wounded and dies after Oenone refuses to heal him.
scenes.stakes: Troy faces ruin from the child; the infant Paris faces death by exposure.

scenes.title: Asopus, Aegina and Aeacus
scenes.summary: Zeus carries off Aegina, and Asopus is driven back by thunderbolts. Her son Aeacus becomes a pious king, and his sons kill Phocus and are exiled.
scenes.stakes: Asopus seeks his stolen daughter; Peleus and Telamon face exile for murder.

scenes.title: Telamon at Salamis
scenes.summary: Telamon takes refuge with Cychreus, inherits Salamis and fathers Ajax, and later Teucer by Hesione.

alias_notes.explanation: Paris was surnamed Alexander for defending the flocks against robbers.

notable_quotes.reason: Hecuba's firebrand dream foretells Troy's burning.
Origin of Cassandra's curse: true prophecy that is never believed.

analysis.text: The chapter shows how genealogy explains Troy's fate, with divine unions, doomed omens and the Palladium shaping the city's rise and fall.
Apollodorus compiles competing local traditions, citing variants for wives and parentage. This reflects how Greek myth varied between regions and authors.

legacy.text: The Palladium became a symbol of a city's protection, and later Romans claimed to keep it in Rome.
Cassandra's cursed prophecy gave the word 'Cassandra' its sense of an unheeded truth-teller.

fun_facts.text: The Library is attributed to Apollodorus but was likely written in the 1st or 2nd century AD.

language_notes.text: "Defile" means to violate or seduce; Iasion's offence was an attempt to force himself on Demeter.
"The opposite mainland" means the Asian coast across the sea from the island of Samothrace.
"Love's dalliance" is a polite way of saying a love affair; Aphrodite slept with the mortal Anchises.
Founding a city where a guiding animal lies down is a common foundation-legend pattern in Greek myth.
A cubit is about eighteen inches, so the image stood roughly four and a half feet tall.
A distaff and spindle are tools for spinning wool, symbols of women's work, paired here with a warlike spear.
The aegis is a protective goatskin garment or shield, an emblem of Zeus and Athena.
"Violation" refers to Zeus's assault; Electra fled to the image for sanctuary.
"The Dawn" is the goddess Eos, who carried off the mortal Tithonus as her lover.

Ilium is Troy. Hercules sacked it earlier after Laomedon cheated him of promised horses; Podarces ("swift-footed") received the name Priam, meaning "ransomed," when Hercules let his sister buy him back.
"Exposed" means left out in the wilderness to die, a common ancient way of disposing of unwanted infants.
Alexander means roughly "defender of men"; the name is explained here by his defending the flocks against robbers.
Cassandra's curse: her prophecies were true but never believed. This explains her later fruitless warnings to the Trojans.
"To wit" is an archaic phrase meaning "namely" or "that is to say," introducing a list.
"Fetch Helen" means to go and bring Helen back as Paris's prize, which in effect meant abducting her.
The coals explanation refers to an ancient belief that the river's coal-like deposits came from Zeus's thunderbolts.
"Cohabited" here is a plain term for sexual union; "begot ... on her" means fathered a child by her.
The ants-into-men story explains the Myrmidons, whose name resembles the Greek word for ants (myrmex).
Psamathe's seal transformation echoes a common myth of sea-deities changing shape to escape pursuers; Phocus's name means "seal".
Aeacus's role as keeper of Hades' keys reflects his tradition as a judge or doorkeeper of the underworld, a reward for his piety.
A quoit is a heavy throwing disc, like a discus.
Ajax's name is linked to the Greek word for eagle (aetos), explaining the naming through the eagle omen.

context_notes.text: Atlas is the Titan who holds up the sky. Zeus fathered Iasion and Dardanus on his daughter Electra.
Aeneas, son of Anchises and Aphrodite, becomes a Trojan hero and, in Roman tradition, the ancestor of Rome.
The Palladium was a sacred image of Pallas on which, in legend, the safety of Troy depended.
Athena's epithet Pallas is traditionally explained by this story of her accidentally killing a companion.
Hecuba's second child is Paris, whose birth is attended by this dream; the firebrand foreshadows Troy burning in the war he causes.
Ida is the mountain near Troy where shepherds pastured flocks. The bear nursing the child is a familiar legendary sign of a hero's special fate.
Philoctetes inherited the bow and poisoned arrows of Hercules; the arrows' poison made wounds incurable except by Oenone's skill.
Ocean and Tethys were Titan sea deities; the genealogy of rivers as their children is standard in Greek myth.
Sisyphus, king of Corinth, was later punished in Hades for his cunning, including, in some accounts, betraying Zeus's secret.
Pelops, ancestor of the Pelopidae, gives his name to the Peloponnese; the story here blames him for a curse on Greece.
Hercules (the Greek Heracles) was Telamon's friend and comrade in the sack of Troy under Laomedon.

literary_notes.text: Iasion's mortal presumption toward a goddess is swiftly punished by a thunderbolt, a typical pattern of crime and divine retribution.
The oracle and the wandering cow anticipate the city's destined founding, giving Ilium a divine sanction from its start.
Athena honors the image with the very aegis that caused Pallas's death, so her grief is bound to the object of her fear.
Hecuba's dream of a firebrand spreading over the city anticipates the burning of Troy because of the child she is carrying.
Apollo's punishment leaves Cassandra with true foresight that nobody believes, a cruel twist on the gift she accepted.
Oenone's change of heart comes too late: she arrives with the cure only to find him dead, making her refusal tragic.
The tale ends by explaining a real feature, the coals in the river, as a lasting trace of divine violence.
This blunt statement establishes Aeacus's defining trait, which the following oracle episode and his afterlife reward.
The pious Aeacus must banish his own sons, a sharp contrast between his virtue and their crime.
